at.step: Reveal: snapshot too old

items.item: Postgres never overwrites a heap tuple in place: an UPDATE is physically a new tuple inserted with its own xmin, while the old tuple stays where it is with its xmax set to the updating transaction — the row is logically one row but physically two tuples until something cleans up the old one.

at.step: Reveal: a real update, inspected directly

items.item: Every heap tuple's fixed 23-byte header carries t_xmin (the inserting transaction's ID) and t_xmax (the deleting/updating transaction's ID) directly in the row itself, so visibility is a property of the tuple, not a separate structure layered on top of it.

at.step: Reveal: a real update, inspected directly

items.item: A transaction's snapshot (pg_current_snapshot) is a data structure recording which transaction IDs were still in-progress at a point in time; a tuple is visible to a reader only if its xmin is outside that in-progress set and its xmax either doesn't apply or is also outside it.

at.step: Reveal: what decides visibility

items.item: Whether a given xmin or xmax actually committed, aborted, or is still in progress is answered by a separate commit-status lookup (pg_xact_status et al.), not by anything stored in the tuple header itself — deciding visibility costs a second read, not just a header comparison.

at.step: Reveal: what decides visibility

items.item: InnoDB and Oracle take the structurally opposite approach: the current row is updated in place at its one physical location, and the value being overwritten is pushed out to a separate undo log (InnoDB) or undo segment (Oracle) before the overwrite happens.

at.step: Reveal: the undo-log family's own answer

items.item: InnoDB's own documentation states plainly that no private copies are created when a transaction writes: only one physical copy of the row exists in the table itself at any time, and the undo log is what lets a concurrent reader reconstruct an older version.

at.step: Reveal: the undo-log family's own answer

items.item: Oracle's own documentation describes reading an older version as active reconstruction work: the database copies the current block, applies undo data to roll it back to the reader's start SCN, and calls the result a 'consistent read (CR) clone' — producing an old version costs CPU work proportional to how much has changed since, not a lookup.

at.step: Reveal: the undo-log family's own answer

items.item: The two families put their real cost in different places and at different times: Postgres pays at write time and after (every update leaves a dead tuple behind that must eventually be reclaimed, previewing the next topic's vacuum), while the undo-log family pays at read time (reconstructing old versions) and bounds how far back a read can reach (the undo log's own retained size).

at.step: Reveal: the real cost of never overwriting

items.item: InnoDB's primary key is the clustered index itself — the table's rows are physically stored in primary-key order at the index's own leaf level — so an in-place update never relocates the row the way Postgres's new-tuple-per-update design does; this is the structural reason the two families' update costs diverge, not merely a configuration difference.

at.step: Reveal: the real cost of never overwriting

items.item: 'Snapshot too old' (Oracle's ORA-01555) is the direct, structural consequence of the undo-log family's bounded, circular history: once other writers' new undo has overwritten the specific undo records a long-running reader still needs, there is nothing left to reconstruct from, and the read fails outright rather than returning stale or inconsistent data.

at.step: Reveal: snapshot too old

items.item: Postgres has no equivalent failure mode by the same mechanism, because a long-running Postgres reader's needed old versions are not a bounded, overwritable log — they are ordinary heap tuples that simply haven't been reclaimed yet; a long read in Postgres can always finish, at the cost of table bloat rather than an outright read failure.

at.step: Reveal: snapshot too old

items.item: Oracle's own documented remedy for ORA-01555 — raising undo_retention, or using larger rollback segments — is literally 'give the bounded log more room before it wraps,' which delays the failure rather than removing the structural cause; Postgres's equivalent mitigation (shortening the long-running read) targets a different resource (bloat) because the underlying mechanism is different.
